summary.text:
£151.0m of the £460.4m book — a third of it — is temporary local-to-local money at 4.62%. In the same report they note that lending into that same market would have earned 4.17%. So Telford is paying 4.62% to borrow from a market it prices at 4.17% on the other side, and it says so openly: the strategy is to hold cheap temporary financing rather than lock in long rates, and it claims more than £30m of cumulative surplus since 2015/16 for doing so.

The liability benchmark shows where that leads — from £448.284m at March 2025 to £649.673m by March 2029, with £74.6m of new borrowing needed in 2026/27 alone. Every step of the table reconciles exactly, as do the debt portfolio components and their 3.80% weighted rate.

A ninth LOBO call for the library: £5m exercised by the lender and repaid.

The MRP policy is the most specific we have read — pre-2007/08 debt divided by 50, Regulation 27(4) used to exclude non-commercial capital loans from MRP entirely, and NuPlace share capital written down over 20 years under Regulation 25(1)(d).

officer.body:
Hi Edward,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the update and 2026/27 strategy that went to Audit Committee in January, recognising your outturn report will have moved things on. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A scope note and a cross-check. What we hold is the mid-year paper, so the actuals below are at 31 December 2025. Your debt portfolio table foots exactly — £279.3m, £30.0m, £0.1m and £151.0m come to £460.4m, and weighting those four rates gives precisely the 3.80% you print. Your liability benchmark reconciles on every step for every forecast year, which is rarer than it should be.

We wrote because of one juxtaposition in your own report. £151.0m of that £460.4m — a third of the book — is temporary local-to-local money at 4.62%. Two pages later you note that investing short term in the local authority market would have returned 4.17%. So you are paying 4.62% to borrow from a market you price at 4.17% on the lending side, and you say so plainly rather than burying it.

That is not a criticism, because your paragraph 3.1 gives the reason and the number behind it: holding cheap temporary financing instead of locking in long rates has generated more than £30m of surplus treasury returns since 2015/16. Against ten-year certainty at 5.83% and twenty-year at 6.38% this afternoon, notice 314/26, that trade is still working. The question your own strategy raises is when it stops, and you have already framed it correctly — the "cost of carry and breakeven analysis" at 4.2.1.

That analysis is exactly what we compute and publish daily, for every council, rather than annually. Both PWLB fixings, all four rate bases, the market-implied Bank Rate path from SONIA — currently 4.11% at one year and 4.21% at two against Bank Rate of 3.75% — and the inter-authority side alongside. We have also just read Wandsworth from the other end of your market: they hold £235m out on deposit to other councils at 4.88% and say authorities are willing to borrow from them well above bank rates. Seeing both sides is the only way to know whether 4.62% was the clearing rate or the expensive end of it. July's PWLB lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin PWLB months are when the temporary market gets dear. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

The scale of what is coming makes it worth watching closely. Your benchmark goes from £448.284m to £649.673m by March 2029 with £74.6m needed in 2026/27 alone, and loan servicing has already moved from 7.85% to a projected 8.34% of net revenue.

Two other things. Your LOBO call — £5m exercised by the lender and repaid — is the ninth we have picked up across the sector in a few months, and every single one was refused or repaid. Oldham published being offered 6.70% and 7.67%; Wolverhampton 6.19% to 6.26%. That is a cross-council picture no council can assemble alone, and it suggests any remaining options in your £30.0m of LOBO and fixed rate loans are more likely to be tested than not.

And your MRP policy at 4.2.3 is the most specific we have read anywhere — pre-2007/08 debt divided by 50 rather than a 4% reducing balance, Regulation 27(4) used to exclude non-commercial capital loans from MRP entirely, and NuPlace share capital written down over 20 years under Regulation 25(1)(d). Most reports we see state a policy in two sentences. If you ever wanted it used as a worked example in our MRP course, we would ask first.

On pricing: your PWLB book sits about £32.6m below par today, and unusually it cuts both ways — 38 loans below and 22 above. Standard caveats: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Telford. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes straight to the £151.0m. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice for the £200m rise ahead. MRP — policy options and revenue impact. And LOBO loans (legacy). All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
